learn.title: Geothermal Energy: Tapping Earth's Inner Heat
learn.intro: Geothermal energy harnesses the Earth's natural heat from deep within its core to generate electricity and provide heating. Unlike solar or wind, it offers consistent baseload power, making it vital for a stable, low-carbon energy future.
learn.c1_text: The Earth’s core reaches temperatures of 6,000°C—hotter than the sun’s surface. Geothermal plants tap underground steam or hot water from reservoirs up to 3 km below ground to spin turbines and generate electricity, much like a natural power plant beneath our feet.
learn.c2_text: Traditional geothermal relies on natural underground reservoirs. Enhanced Geothermal Systems (EGS) inject water into hot dry rock to create artificial reservoirs. This expands geothermal potential beyond tectonic zones, potentially unlocking vast energy resources across more regions.
learn.c3_text: India has an estimated 20 GW of geothermal potential, mainly in the Himalayan region. The government included geothermal in its renewable energy mix, though development lags behind solar and wind. Pilot projects in Himachal Pradesh and Arunachal Pradesh are underway to explore commercial viability.
learn.stat1: Global geothermal capacity reached 15.4 GW in 2023, supplying ~0.3% of global electricity.
learn.stat2: Iceland generates over 25% of its total electricity from geothermal sources.
learn.stat3: Enhanced geothermal could provide up to 100 GW globally by 2050.
learn.stat4: India ranks 7th globally in geothermal resource potential.

learn.title: Tidal Stream Energy: Predictable Ocean Power
learn.intro: Tidal stream energy captures power from moving water currents caused by gravitational forces between Earth, Moon, and Sun. Unlike unpredictable renewables, tides are highly predictable—offering reliable, clean energy for coastal nations and island grids.
learn.c1_text: Tidal stream turbines resemble underwater wind turbines, anchored to the seabed in fast-flowing tidal channels. With over 800 times the density of air, water allows these turbines to generate power efficiently even at low speeds, making them ideal for predictable energy generation.
learn.c2_text: Tides follow predictable cycles governed by lunar physics, enabling accurate energy forecasting decades ahead. This reliability contrasts sharply with solar and wind, allowing grid operators to schedule tidal generation like conventional power plants, enhancing grid stability and reducing backup needs.
learn.c3_text: India’s 7,500 km coastline hosts several sites suitable for tidal energy, particularly in the Gulf of Kutch and along the Bay of Bengal. The Ministry of New and Renewable Energy has identified pilot zones, aiming to harness 1 GW of tidal power by 2030 as part of its ocean energy roadmap.
learn.stat1: Global tidal stream resource potential is estimated at 120 TWh annually—enough for 115 million homes.
learn.stat2: The MeyGen project in Scotland is the world’s largest tidal stream array, producing 6 GWh since 2017.
learn.stat3: Tidal currents can reach speeds exceeding 5 m/s in prime locations, offering high energy density.
learn.stat4: India’s theoretical tidal energy potential is around 120 GW, though only a fraction is currently exploitable.

learn.title: Carbon Markets: Pricing Pollution to Cut Emissions
learn.intro: Carbon markets put a price on greenhouse gas emissions, creating financial incentives for businesses to reduce pollution. By capping total emissions and trading allowances, these systems drive investment toward cleaner technologies and accelerate the shift to a net-zero economy.
learn.c1_text: In cap-and-trade systems, governments set a declining limit on total emissions and issue permits accordingly. Companies bidding for credits must either cut pollution or buy allowances. This creates a market-driven incentive to innovate and invest in clean alternatives faster than regulation alone.
learn.c2_text: Carbon credits represent one tonne of CO₂ avoided or removed. Companies can purchase verified credits from renewable projects, reforestation, or carbon capture initiatives to meet compliance obligations. This flexibility lowers abatement costs while funding sustainable development globally.
learn.c3_text: India launched its national carbon market in 2021 under the Perform, Achieve and Trade (PAT) cycle. Initially covering 1,100 industrial units, it plans to expand sector-wide. The government also supports international carbon credit exports through rooftop solar and wind projects under old Kyoto mechanisms.
learn.stat1: The global carbon market was valued at $2.8 trillion in 2023, according to the World Bank.
learn.stat2: India’s first domestic emissions trading scheme targets 5% annual emission reductions across covered sectors.
learn.stat3: Over 40 countries now operate some form of cap-and-trade system covering ~22% of global emissions.
learn.stat4: Voluntary carbon markets transacted $2 billion worth of credits in 2023.

learn.title: Wave Energy Converters: Harvesting Ocean Swells
learn.intro: Wave energy converters transform the rhythmic motion of ocean waves into electricity. With the world’s waves holding enough energy to power countries multiple times over, this emerging technology promises clean, renewable power without the visual impact of offshore wind farms.
learn.c1_text: Point absorbers use floating buoys that move with waves, driving hydraulic pistons or generators below deck. Overtopping devices capture swells in reservoirs, releasing them through turbines. These systems operate best in open oceans with consistent wave climates, offering scalable marine energy solutions.
learn.c2_text: Modern wave converters use either direct-drive linear generators or hydraulic systems. Hydraulic designs convert wave motion into pressurized fluid, spinning hydraulic motors connected to generators. Direct-drive systems reduce mechanical complexity but require robust materials to withstand saltwater corrosion long-term.
learn.c3_text: India’s National Institute of Ocean Technology is testing wave energy prototypes off the Kerala coast. The Ministry of New and Renewable Energy supports R&D under its Ocean Energy program, targeting demonstration projects by 2026. India’s 7,500 km coastline presents significant untapped wave energy potential.
learn.stat1: Worldwide wave energy potential exceeds 29,000 TWh per year—triple current global electricity demand.
learn.stat2: The European Marine Energy Centre tests over 30 wave energy technologies annually in Scotland.
learn.stat3: India’s coastal states receive average wave heights of 1.5–3 meters, suitable for energy extraction.
learn.stat4: Global wave energy market is projected to reach $129 million by 2030, growing at 10% CAGR.

learn.title: Flow Batteries: Storing Renewables at Scale
learn.intro: Flow batteries store energy in liquid electrolytes held in external tanks, enabling long-duration discharge essential for balancing intermittent renewables. Their scalable architecture and rapid response make them key for stabilizing grids powered increasingly by solar and wind.
learn.c1_text: Vanadium redox flow batteries use vanadium ions dissolved in sulfuric acid, offering long cycle life and stable performance. Iron-chromium systems are cheaper but less efficient. Both store energy in tanks, allowing independent scaling of power and capacity—an advantage over lithium-ion for multi-hour storage needs.
learn.c2_text: Unlike traditional batteries where energy and power scale together, flow batteries separate these metrics. Increasing tank size boosts stored energy, while adding stacks raises output power. This modular design suits large-scale grid applications requiring 4–10 hours of storage, unlike short-cycle lithium systems.
learn.c3_text: India’s Ministry of New and Renewable Energy funds flow battery research through its STORAGE scheme. Startups like Exicom and Tata Chemicals are developing vanadium-based prototypes. Pilot projects aim to integrate flow batteries with solar microgrids in Rajasthan and Gujarat for rural electrification.
learn.stat1: Global flow battery market reached $380 million in 2023 and is expected to exceed $1.7 billion by 2030.
learn.stat2: Vanadium flow batteries offer over 20,000 cycles with minimal degradation, lasting decades.
learn.stat3: India plans to deploy 40 GWh of grid-scale storage by 2030, including emerging technologies like flow batteries.
learn.stat4: A typical utility-scale flow battery can store 10–100 MWh of energy for 10+ hours.

learn.title: Green Hydrogen: Electrolysis for Clean Fuel
learn.intro: Green hydrogen is produced by splitting water using renewable electricity, yielding zero-emission fuel for hard-to-abate sectors like steelmaking, shipping, and heavy transport. As nations seek carbon neutrality, green hydrogen bridges clean power generation and industrial decarbonization.
learn.c1_text: Proton Exchange Membrane (PEM) electrolyzers use solid polymer membranes and operate at high pressure, ideal for variable renewables due to fast response. Alkaline systems rely on liquid potassium hydroxide, are cheaper but slower. Both split water into H₂ and O₂ using clean electricity efficiently.
learn.c2_text: Large-scale green hydrogen requires massive electrolyzer deployments powered by dedicated renewables. Challenges include managing explosive hydrogen gas, preventing embrittlement in pipelines, and ensuring purity standards. Safety protocols and materials science innovations are critical for safe handling and transport infrastructure development.
learn.c3_text: Launched in 2023, India’s $2.3 billion Green Hydrogen Mission targets 5 MMT annual production by 2030. It offers subsidies for domestic manufacturing and mandates blending in fertilizers and steel sectors. Major players like Reliance and IOCL plan gigawatt-scale electrolyzer plants powered by solar and wind.
learn.stat1: India aims to produce 5 million tonnes of green hydrogen annually by 2030 under its National Green Hydrogen Mission.
learn.stat2: Global green hydrogen demand could reach 50 million tonnes by 2050, per IEA Net Zero Scenario.
learn.stat3: PEM electrolyzers cost $800–1,200/kW today, down from $1,500/kW in 2020.
learn.stat4: Australia, Germany, and Japan lead in green hydrogen export plans, investing over $30 billion collectively.
